>>
it [the BIN file] can be encoded out to 300 or 2000 baud formats.
>>

That is incorrect.  Currently Ballybin can only work with 2000 baud programs (the 300 baud interface is extremely hard to find anyway).  The 300 baud programs that we archive are converted to 2000 baud, since it's so much faster.  With many 300 baud programs the sound is messed-up (not the fault of archiving, but the sound is setup differently between the two BASICs).  If you want to hear the sound correctly under "300 baud" Bally BASIC, then load the program using AstroBASIC (at 2000 baud) and then switch BASIC cartridges using the "swap method" (it's the reverse method of how we archive a 300-baud tape).  It's a little weird switching BASIC carts, but once you get the hang of it, it's a breeze (and faster than loading a program at 300 baud!).  The description on how to do this is in the "BASIC - Documents" folder.  The filename is "cartridge_conversion.txt."

The Game Player, #5  -- Vol. 5, pg. 62, February 18, 1983

Michael Prosise has some fun with . . .

   NAM-CAP
   New Image, Tape #1500

    Whacka-whacka-whacka???... Yes!  Has the little yellow gobbler finally made it to BALLY/ASTROCADE?  Well-l-l-l, a hint is in this game's title, which might be spelled backwards.
    Don Gladden of NEW IMAGE has come up with quite an entertaining version (in reverse) of the popular Midway coin-op PACMAN.  In fact, there are six variations of NAM-CAP on the cassette, each unique in it's own way.
    So what is a NAM-CAP you might be wondering.  To use Don's words, the little guy finally ate too many dots and ghosts.  Now he's spitting them out! The object of this game is to FILL the maze with dots.
    What NEW IMAGE has done is take the PAC-MAN game concept and reversed it.  You have a maze, with tunnels on each side, that is devoid of dots.  You steer the NAMCAP guy through the maze, trying to fill it with dots, while simultaneously avoiding the pursuing block-shaped object.  During the chase, your guy will, of it's own doing, deposit a stationary ghost at three different places that neither you or your pursuer may pass through.  To attempt this will mean your destruction.
    NAM-CAP is for one to four players, is in color, and offers the choice of one to ten turns.  The graphics are good; in fact, the ghosts are just like the one's in PACMAN.  There are several different mazes.  A new one will appear each time you complete one.  In the six versions, the speed of movement is faster than some of the others.  In version four, you disappear after 500 points, the maze disappears at 1000 points and after 1500 points both disappear!  It's fun.
    Of the PAC-MAN type games that have appeared so far for the BALLY/ASTROCADE, NAMCAP is probably the closest to the coin-op as far as feel of play and visual aspects are concerned.  Although the maze layout is different, it functions just as well.  Those who played it liked it quite a bit.  They even thought it was better than Wavemaker's PACK RAT.  The sound effects are nice also, and another good feature is that high score of the day, along with the final score for all players, is displayed at the end of each game.
    NAM-CAP is fun to play, much like PAC-MAN, and should be available by the time you read this.

Typing and Archiving 'Cavern Quest'

Though I've had an Astrocade since 1994, I've never typed in a full program.   I thought that I'd change that today.  I typed in "Cavern Quest" By Bruce Jaeger which was in the July 1983 issue of Creative Computing magazine.  I expected it to take a few hours (with that little keypad!), but it didn't take that long at all.  Here's a rundown of how long it took:

1) Started typing "Cavern Quest" at 9:55AM
2) At 10:21 I'm on line 21; I backup what's done so far.
3) :PRINT and :LIST at 10:22 - Verifies okay
4) At 10:29 begin line 21
5) :PRINT and :LIST at 10:54 - Verifies okay
6) At 10:57 begin line 38
7) Finished typing program 11:20
8) :PRINT and :LIST at 11:23 - Verifies okay
9) RUN for first time at 11:24
10) Fixed error in line 1 - Typed "/" "but it's supposed to
   be the divide sign on the Astrocade
11) RUN for second time at 11:27 - program takes about one
   minute to create maze.
12) Beat game at 12:35 - Needed to make a map

It took me about an hour and twenty minutes to type-in the program; not bad considering I took my time making backups and making (and drinking) tea.  It took me an hour and ten minutes to beat the game.  I'd call that a fair time exchange.  The game could be beat much faster if you don't make a map and just run in random directions-- but what would be the fun in that?

The program has been archived as cavern_quest.zip and can be found here:

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/ballyalley/files/Tapes%20-%20Programs/Games/

1316:
Hints on Archiving Tapes with Ballybin
--------------------------------------

Since I've been archiving Astrocade tapes using Ballybin and Astrowav, I've learned a few tricks that make it much easier.  Here they are:

1) Save an entire tape as a WAV file, rather than one program
  at a time.  Load the WAV file into some sound editor (I use
  Cool Edit) and save each program as a separate file.  Once
  the programs are separated, it's time to clean them up.
  Listen to WAV file; delete all static and silence up to the
  first header tone.  Also delete the static and silence after
  the footer tone.  If the program isn't part of a menu system,
  now run Ballybin-- the program should archive fine.

2) If the program you want to archive is part of a menu system,
  then it is best to remove the few bytes that tell the menu
  which program it is.  Sometimes Ballybin will do this for
  you, without the need to do it by hand, but more often than
  not, Ballybin will see the first couple of bytes and only
  archive them-- not the actual program.  Open the WAV file
  in a sound editor.  Listen closely to the file; you will hear
  a short burst of bytes, followed by more "header tone."  What
  you've just heard is a complete "program."  It has its own
  separate header and footer tone.  You want to delete that
  descriptive menu program.  Using your sound editor, zoom in
  about a second after you hear that very short burst of progam.
  You will see a VERY brief interval between the footer tone of
  the first program and the header tone of the actual program
  that you want to archive.  Delete that menu program, all the
  way from the beginning of the file to the end of the footer
  tone.  This sounds more complicated that it is: once you see
  the program in a sound editor, listen, and than zoom in, it's
  very simple.

3) If Ballybin isn't archiving the whole program, but does
  archive part of it (and you've ruled out that -l on the
  command line doesn't help), then resave the program as a
  WAV file, but this time turn the Tone on the stereo way up.
  This sometimes helps to sort it out.

If you have any other hints, reply to this message.  We'll add them all together into one FAQ file.

Adam

On Astro Bugs Tapes 3-5

Archiving is not as easy as one, two, three; there is quite a bit of time and effort going on behind the archiving effort.  Thanks Lance, for archiving these programs and typing in the instructions (I corrected spelling errors and re-uploaded the zip file).

I tried out each program, here's what I thought:

10,000 RND Boxes (Tape 3) - There are many BASIC demos that use random lines or boxes to, well, just show something on the screen.  I don't see anything different that makes this program stand out from other programs that do the same thing (it might be a little faster?).  This one does play some short "music" after a screen is finished, but there's no reason to have it there.  If you have not seen a random box program before, then you can't go wrong with this one, it'll give you your fill.

Rescue Force (Tape 3) - This is a Choplifter clone, and a rather good one at that.  I was a bit frustrated at first on how to land without crashing, but I eventually got the hang of it.  Reading the instructions gives you some sci-fi background, but you don't need it to play.  I like that this game sticks to its title.  Since you're rescuing people, there is no reason for guns, so the trigger has no effect in this game.

Star Base II (Tape 5) - A scrolling game.  The concept is good (shoot your way through obstacles in space), but the game has flaws.  First off, there is too much empty space to fly through at the beginning of the game.  If I were shooting at enemies then that would be fine, but there are no enemies; the ship is just cruising along.  Secondly, the shots fired from the ship don't go far enough.  You have to wait until you are very close to the obstacle before you can hit it.  Thirdly, and most damning of all, the ship has to be maneuvered through corridors that are only as wide as the ship, and the ship isn't easy to control (plus it takes three shots to open a corridor, and you barely have time to make those shots!).  This game is worth trying, but I think that the author bit off more than AstroBASIC could chew.

Yearly Income (Tape 4) - I loaded it; it works.  I didn't try this program; I would be worried about myself if I had.  This machine was called The Bally Arcade: has anyone ever seen a program like this in the arcades?  You haven't, and you never will.  There's a reason for that...

I checked out Super Slope; it's a good game.  After playing so many BASIC games lately, it's quite a shock to see four colors.  Really.  The game plays well, but it has the exact same problem that the version on the multicart has: your skier often leaves part of himself behind, so you'll end up with half-a-guy coasting down the hill.  Mike and I talked about this problem a while back; this isn't a bad archive: that's just the way this game is.

If you can get over all the "garbage" on the side of the screen, then this is a descent play.  Of all the programs that have been archived so far, Super Slope is the closest to "cartridge quality."  That doesn't make it the BEST game, but since the character is easy to control, the animation is smooth, and it makes good use of colors, it does have a lot going for it.  The drawback is that most players will see the sides of the screen and wonder what the heck is going on (if you haven't tried it yet, load it and you'll see what I mean).  If you've played Skiing on the Atari 2600, then you will see that this game is more of the same.  You'll have the hang of Super Slope in minutes and be looking for something with more variety.

From Arcadian, Vol. 5, No. 3, Pg. 49 (Jan. 14, 1983)

SNEAK UP AND BITE YA DEPARTMENT
-------------------------------
By Hoover Anderson Research and Design (H.A.R.D.)

By the time that volume 1, number 6 of ARCADIAN had hit the streets (May 1979) it was apparent that there were two configurations of on-board ROM.  Calls to some ROM subroutines worked on some machines but not on others.

H.A.R.D. has just spent an exasperating two months trying to produce game tapes in 2000 baud Astrobasic that would load on the customer's machine.  The problem was that all PRINT statements in our programs were producing characters that were offset by one letter AND one pixel on our customer's machines: the string "ABC" would come out "BCD" and slightly off-center.

At first we thought it might be the tape quality.  We spent a bundle having custom cassettes loaded with high-quality Agfa PE-651 tape.  No good... the problem remained.  We next suspected the recorder.  Out went the trusty old Panasonic Slimline to be replaced by a TRS-80 CCR-81 computer cassette recorder.  Still no dice... the characters remained jumbled on everyone else's machine but our own.  That was the worst part... we couldn't duplicate the problem!  Everything loaded worked perfectly in our own shop.  At the suggestion of one of our dealers , we even tried a new Astrobasic cartridge.  No deal... the problem would not go away.  Finally, in desperation, we bought another Arcade.  Aha!  We now had to Arcades sitting side by side on the bench, and they couldn't talk to each other!  There ARE two different types of Arcades out there.  The difference lies in the on-board ROM, which is five bytes off-standard between the two.  I have christened these two machines "The 3159" and the "3164" based on the address of the "GAME OVER" character string in each.  A machine-language monitor dump of the ROM was changed.  Who knows why?... there was a bug fixed, perhaps.  Most of you have the 3159, but there are a number of you with the 3164 machines who are tearing your hear out or perhaps giving up in disgust because you can't load anyone else's programs.

Here's a quick test.  Type in the following on your Arcade:

CLEAR; %(19904)=-43;%(19906)=12341;%(19908)=27651;%(19910)=3164;%(19912)=-13871; CALL19904

If the words "GAME OVER" appear at the top of your screen, you've got the 3164 configuration and you are stuck.  The newer 3159 configuration will only print the word "OVER".  If you change %(19910) to 3159, you will get the entire "GAME OVER" on the 3159 machine.

END OF ARTICLE

This article is from a 1979 issue of the Arcadian.  It explains (well) how BASIC uses the "screen" to store a program.  This topic seems to come up often; this article explains everything anyone could ask about the subject.

Adam


Bally Astrocade Screen Operations
By John Perkins

The screen is divided into a left and a right side with a movable boundary.  The following outputs prevail:

    &(0)=right side register 0    &(4)=left side register 0
    &(1)=right side register 1    &(5)=left side register 1
    &(2)=right side register 2    &(6)=left side register 2
    &(3)=right side register 3    &(7)=left side register 3

    +--+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+
    |     Color    |  Shade |
    +--+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+
       Color Register Byte

    Background  /----------------
    Area        | +-------|------
     |          | |       *-------- Left/Right Color Boundary
     +-----------*|       |
                | |       |  +----- Memory Partition
                | |       |  |
                | +-------|--*---
                \----------------

Bally BASIC continually sets &(4) and &(5) to the color/shade defined by BC [Background Color], and &(6) and &(7) to the color/shade defined by FC [Foreground Color].  These are fixed while BASIC is in control.  But by moving the boundary so that the right side is visible, we can then control four different color/shades by using the &(0) thru &(3).  [Type this] example [into BASIC]:

    &(0)=30;&(1)=85;&(2)=153;&(3)=125;&(9)=0

Three colors are displayed- listing, background, and "garbage" at the top (more on this later).  The fourth color should be visible as we scroll the text into the upper border area.  With &(9) at some other value, such as 10, the screen is divided and the FC and BC [BASIC] commands allow two more colors on the screen.  Actually, &(9) has two functions:

    +------+------+------+------+------+------+------+------+
    | Right Back- |               Left/Right                |
    | ground Color|             Color Boundary              |
    +------+------+------+------+------+------+------+------+
       Register 9 [Sets Left/Right color mapping boundary]

The least significant six bits set the boundary position (four pixels or one memory byte per unit).  The most significant two bits choose the color register associated with the left side background and the right side background.  Try [typing this example in BASIC after having tried the first example]:

    &(9)=135.

The "garbage" mentioned above is actually the stored program, in the screen memory, using the even bit positions.

    +--------+---------+--------+---------+
    | Screen | Program | Screen | Program |
    +--------+---------+--------+---------+...
      Odd Bit  Even Bit  Odd Bit  Even Bit ...

Each pixel equates to two bits of memory- 4 pixels to an 8 bit byte.  The two bits of each pixel can have four representations:

    00 = &(4) left    or   &(0) right
    01 = &(5) left    or   &(l) right
    10 = &(6) left    or   &(2) right
    11 = &(7) left    or   &(3) right

When Bally BASIC sets the screen boundary ( &(9) ) all the way to the right, then only the left registers &(4) to &(7) are used.  Since it also sets &(4) and &(5) to BC, and &(6) and &(7) to FC, only the odd bits of memory show on the screen.

    00 is the same color as 01
    10 is the same color as 11

By storing the program in the even bits it can occupy screen memory (as every other bit) and yet be invisible.  However, by moving the boundary to the left, the right-side registers are used, and since the program above set these to different colors, the stored program becomes "visible" as the garbage at the top of the screen.

&(10) controls how many raster lines are displayed from memory as opposed to being part of the background. &(10)=204 displays all of memory (RAM) allowing visual inspection of the running program.


Note: Original article informatiion:

- Perkins, John "Tutorial (1)  Screen Operations," ARCADIAN, 1, no. 6 (May 1979): 40.


End of article

ADAM - I was hoping to get in touch with Mike and Marion [of Spectre].  I would like to ask them about releasing BLAST DROIDS into the public domain as well as your two programs.  I think that would be the last of the three (?) Esoterica, Inc cartridges.

Esoterica was only the distributor of our cartridges. They distributed other peoples products as well. I don't remember Blast Droids, so I'm pretty sure it was someone else's. (I wrote a lot of programs around that time, and if Esoterica took one and made a cartridge out of it - giving it a new name - then they did it without our permission.)

ADAM - Not only do I want to ask them that, but I would like to hear about how they set up the company and more.  Let me know if I can contact them (email preferred).

BRETT - I can give you a little background on that.

Originally there was four of us. The fourth was Dana Adams, a GREAT artist.  But Dana joined the Air Force and left our group...

Brett  - engineer/programmer (Bally/TRS-80/etc...)
Dana   - artist/programmer (TRS-80)
Marion - musician/programmer (TRS-80)
Mike   - manager

We started writing programs for the TRS-80. Crunch Bug, Black Box, etc... But they were all black and white and bored the crap out of me... :-)

Since the Bally shared the same processor (Z-80), it was an easy jump for me to take a Bally apart, reverse engineer it, disassemble the ROM and map out the software calls, and then reverse engineer Bally's custom BASIC's.

We used the TRS-80 as our assembler for the games. And once we started generating object code, we realized that if we mapped the Bally slot space into the TRS-80 Expansion memory map (and wired it up as such), we would have a 'real-time' development environment for the Bally Arcade. All we had to do was target the TRS-80 Expansion RAM space for the object code, hit reset on the Bally, and it would then 'execute' the code from the TRS-80 as if it were a cartridge. At the same time, the TRS-80 was still able to examine and change memory locations, so we could 'tweak' the parameters of the game on the fly.

Ah, life was fun then...

ADAM - As for other Astrocade stuff... The Bally Alley site is coming along well... Lance Squire, creator of the original Astrocade FAQ recently contacted me (after me searching for him for years)... Don Gladden contacted me... and I'm still looking for others.

BRETT - You should also contact George Moses, one of the 'old gang' of the Bally Bugs... George helped rewrite the Bally Basic manual, and when I wrote the three voice music program, George wrote music for it...

END OF ARTICLE

I got some comments (via email) from Stefano on the Astrocade FAQ; his is my reply to him.  It's general for the whole group, so I'm posting it:

Differences between MESS and Astrocade:

1) The sound isn't 100% (Frank knows this already, and plans to fix it at some point).  Until you compare some games side by side you won't even notice... but SOME carts are missing a sound or two-- or a sound is not quite right.  Now you probably want a list of which carts... I can't think of any right now (Maybe Tests?).  I discovered a missing sound when I was disassembling Dogpatch, so that's one cart you can compare.  Until I disassembles it, I didn't even notice the sound was gone.  It wasn't until I went and listened for it that I noticed it was missing.  I bet there are several carts like this.

2) MESS Memory Expansion is there to some degree- I'm not sure how much (it might even be a "left over" from MAME).  For instance, since the Bally only has 4K some carts don't work without extra RAM (if you plug them in you get a blank screen).  These carts will work with MESS (Blue Ram BASIC 1.1, Vipersoft BASIC).

3) MESS doesn't allow you to switch carts and not lose RAM.  Normally, this wouldn't even make sense to do, but some carts REQUIRE this.  Blue Ram Utility and some other homebrew "from tape" carts work like this on a real Astrocade: 1) Insert Cart 1, say, Blue Ram Utility.  Astrocade goes into loop and doesn't look for ejected cart. 2) Eject Cart, and put in whichever BASIC is requested. 3) Press the keypad key that is requested and the program runs.  This method was devised in about 1985 so that the Blue Ram Utility wouldn't have to be loaded from tape all of the time.

4) The MESS keypad emulation is hard to use for most people.  This is what people complain about most about the MESS emulator.  I can't say that I'm used to the keypad emulation, but at least I can use it.  If there were an easier way, I would love it.  I even wrote a FAQ about the emulation, and at the end of it I suggested some ways that might work better (other than the obvious- use the keyboard so that A=A, etc).

Comments on what you mentioned:

1) Tape emulation - This is a must.  Now that there are some seventy BASIC tapes archived, this should be added.  Bob Fabris's program Ballybin turns a WAV file into a binary.  When he wrote Ballybin he thought that the binary might eventually be used for emulation, so he set it up for that.  (That's about all I know about it.)

2) Memory cards (BTW which sizes are supported) - I don't see what anything up to 64K can't be emulated.  I'm not suggesting emulating the extra features of the 64K RAM Board, or the Blue Ram; just giving the machine access to 64K.  Sort of as if there was 64K hanging off the 50 pin connector of the Astrocade itself.

3) ICBM controller - Since ICBM Attack is one of a VERY few amount of PD Astrocade games, it would be nice if it were playable; you sure have a point in bringing this up.  I wouldn't have thought of mentioning it.

4) Light pen - This was never released, though there were homebrew versions of it.  There is even a program in the Arcadian that requires a homebrew lightpen.  I'm not sure what the point of emulating it would be...

Some notes on your other questions:

equiparable? I.e. can programs written for Blue Ram work on a machine with
Viper installed (and vice versa)

Blue Ram BASIC would work with the Viper 1, or the 64K RAM board, so any programs written for that language could be used on any machine with memory expansion.  I know that the RAM boards are not 100% compatable.  For instance, the RAM for the Viper 1 begins in the $5000 area, while the RAM for the Blue Ram begins in the $6000 area (or vice versa?).  I don't know much about that though...

Not quite at machine launch, but not terribly long thereafter.  The Add-on was first shown at the 1979 Winter CES in Vegas.  Both Jay Fenton (when he was still Jay) and I attended and were responsible for the care & upkeep of the Add-on/Arcade combination.  The language was TERSE, an acronym which stood for: 'Terse Efficient Reentrant Stack Engine', authored by Alan McNeal, also responsible for the built-in Gunfight Game, and also Stern's Berzerk and Frenzy coin-op.

>2.Tom DeFanti arrived, he and Jay put ZGrass on one of these units.

>3. A stand alone unit was created for Tom's group.


The standalone was actually a box built for developing games, which I believe evolved into the UV1.


>  4.We really don't
>know what management was playing at re the keyboard.

I think 'management' or, perhaps more accurately, mis-management, was already giving up on the Add-on shortly after that CES show.  The machine got a very good reaction, and a marketeer (no, not the kind with the big, round ears... but close) and I went on a west coast tour to show the machine to Bally distributors.  We stopped in LA, SF, and Seattle.  I believe the decision had already been made to can it by then, and the trip was merely a formality, and I quit shortly thereafter since it was obvious the Add-on had been dropped.  The reason?  Poor reliability of the base unit due to overheating of the data chip and not enough design margin in the power supply.  Hard to sell a lot of Add-ons when the basic unit kept coming back for repair.  Midway (who built it) had a rather large 'bone-pile'.  They were not used to having to fix anything they produced, the distributors took care of that.  It was different with the consumer product.

The data chip overheated for two reasons:

1.      7.15 MHz was pushing it for a clock speed with 7 micron or so NMOS
2.      The video DACs used a resistor network which dissipated a fair amount of power.

This was made worse by the requirement to shield the entire board to get it to pass FCC, which was a new requirement for manufacturers at the time.  We had quite a difficult time shielding the connection between the Arcade and the Add-on, which probably was another factor in the Add-on's demise.  Since the Arcade cabinet had already been hard-tooled (at quite an expense) there was no way the cabinet was going to be modified to improve cooling or shielding.  All that stuff had to be shoe-horned into the existing cabinet, resulting in the reliability problems we've all experienced.  The Add-on was a bit easier, since it was (at least for the prototypes) just bent sheet metal, having its' own intrinsic shielding (and heat dissipating qualities).  We did use a bit of copper foil to seal up seams between the Add-on's case and top panel, though, adding to cost.

> Actually it is overscan. If you adjust the vertical hold till you can see the black space between the bottom and top of a picture frame, you will see that there is also a line and a bit of text at the top!

What you may not have noticed is that the text is shifted 1/2 a line to the right.

Try this:

10CLEAR ;&(10)=255
20 PRINT "1111111111111111
11111111112222222222222222
22222222223333333333333333
3333333333"

Now adjust the vertical hold till you can see the black line, and what is happening becomes visable.

&(10)=255 tells the video(DATA) chip to continue displaying data well beyond the limitations of the on board ram, AND I might add the documented limits of the display.

When the video(DATA) chip hits the end of ram it loops back to the top and continues drawing data. The data is shifted 1/2 screen probabily because of the Arcade allowing for the 1/2 line of second field video at the bottom of a normal display. You should see the 1/2 lines at the top and bottom of the black line.

The 1s row is shifted, but fist nicely into the 1/2 line before the black. The 2s line is in the black area. The 3s line is at the top of the screen (below the black line) with 1.5 pixels of the > prompt displayed below that.

Next is a breaf white space, where the DATA chip(video) resets its self to start a new display, then the actual 3 lines we printed.

NOW,

In theroy, if we change the top lines of ram after the scan has passed, but before the chip hits the end of ram, we could continue the display off the bottom of the screen.

The real trick would be to replace the actual top of display before the chip got back to it.

On my Commodore 1701 monitor, I can clearly see the top half of the ones line and the bottom half of the threes line, plus the extra bits. Your motitor/tv may vary.

In most shooters the enemys move along pre programed paths, usually using a sin table, rather than computing the values, or alternatly, moving at a set rate in one direction while doubeling the rate in the other to a point then halfing it till the original rate. This would look simular to a sine wave but simply use shift multiply/divide.

For most any angle the vector routines in the Bally rom would work. However you may need to calculate the vector.

Back to my line draw...

If we wanted a line from 0,0 to 10,25, we first find the shorter distance 0-10 and divide it by the longer distance 25.

This gives us a Vector of 0.4 in the X direction.

placing 0.4 into VX and 1.0 into VY and ploting 25 outputs from the vector routines will give you that line, or move your sprite along that path.
